title: A History of Violence
full_review:
Like "The Road to Perdition," this latest adaptation of a graphic novel is a doom-laden tale of murder and retribution.

"A History of Violence" (New Line) concerns an upstanding Indiana family man, Tom Stall (Viggo Mortensen), who becomes a local hero after he faces down the cold-blooded killers who hold up his diner. The film opens with them leaving a motel after slaughtering the workers inside, so when they show up at Stall's Diner, you know they want more than a burger and fries.

Tom has already been shown to be a good -- almost saintly -- father with a devoted lawyer wife, Edie (Maria Bello), a young daughter, Sarah (Heidi Hayes), and a 10th-grader son, Jack (Ashton Holmes), who's the even-tempered target of a couple of sadistic bullies.

Tom's heroic stand brings him national television coverage, much to his embarrassment, but just as the publicity calms down, he's visited at the diner by scar-faced underworld kingpin Carl Fogarty (Ed Harris), who insists Stall had once been a gangster with another name who caused his disfigurement years before in Philadelphia.

Tom and Edie protest that Fogarty is mistaken, and that Tom has never even been to that city, but Fogarty -- backed by his two goons -- continues to menace the Stall family.
Between the gang's ominous presence and the bullies at school, who seem scarcely less deadly in their sadistic taunting, you know something bad is going to happen. And indeed it does, in spite of the Stalls' solid friendship with the capable local sheriff (Peter MacNeill).

But to say more would ruin a film that abounds in nuanced revelations.

David Cronenberg demonstrates his skill in a masterfully crafted psychological drama with a screenplay by Josh Olson, loosely based on John Wagner and Vince Locke's original work. The sharp photography by Peter Suschitzky is another asset.

The story has overtones of those classic Westerns in which the peaceable protagonist must resort to force against implacable evil, or films such as "The Desperate Hours" in which a decent family is confronted by brutish thugs, not to mention numerous other films where men of conscience try to escape their fate.

"Violence" features first-rate acting (including William Hurt), but despite its arguably redemptive ending, the violence quotient -- and stomach-churning suspense -- means the film won't be for every taste.

Maintaining a taut mood throughout, Cronenberg doesn't wallow in brutality; each act is dispatched with speed and is integral to the plot, but there's no denying the number of bodies that pile up. Apart from the murderous deeds of the criminal characters, the other killings all fall under the heading of self-defense. The savagery isn't glorified, but shown in its ugliness, even when, as in several instances here, it is justified.

To say that the film shows the effects of violence on a family as well as a community seems to be stating the obvious, but the results are thought-provoking. All the characters are eventually forced to reveal aspects of themselves not apparent from the start.

Mortensen -- so different from his role in "The Lord of the Rings" -- makes a fine average Joe caught in a nightmarish quagmire.

There are also two mostly clothed sexual encounters between Tom and Edie. One, early on, playful; the second, when tensions are at fever pitch, extremely violent, though actual nudity is minimal. Both scenes are dramatically meaningful, but be warned: They're strong.

The film contains much profanity, rough and crude language, violence with gore, including several murders, two graphic husband-wife sexual encounters (one quite brutal), drug use, and full frontal female and rear male nudity. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is L -- limited adult audience, films whose problematic content many adults would find troubling. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.
